national.title: Maps show where Thanksgiving storms could disrupt holiday
national.summary: Rain, snow and powerful winds were forecast to impact large stretches of the country on Thanksgiving, potentially disrupting holiday festivities and, in some areas, hampering travel plans.
national.body: Various types of severe weather are expected to impact large stretches of the United States this week, potentially disrupting Thanksgiving plans and hampering travel for Americans along both coasts and into the middle of the country.A storm developing Wednesday over Florida threatened to bring flooding to southeastern states before quickly traveling up the coast and moving into the Northeast in time for Thanksgiving. Forecasts showed the storm could generate high winds and heavy rain across the region, while areas in the Midwest, including St. Louis, could see snow around the holiday.In New York City, organizers of the iconic Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade announced the parade is being postponed until Saturday due to the coming storm. It's the first time in the parade's 100-year history that it's been postponed, although it was not held at all from 1942 to 1944 because of World War II. In 1971, the balloons were grounded due to strong winds, but the parade still went on.While the city isn't expected to get excessive rain, a relatively rare High Wind Warning was issued, and wind gusts could reach 60 mph.New York Gov. Kathy Hochul on Wednesday night declared a state of emergency for New York City, along with Nassau, Suffolk and Westchester counties. "We're expecting heavy rain and strong winds that could create dangerous travel conditions," she wrote on social media. And in a travel advisory, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani stated that forecasts showed the worst of the storm would likely hit the city beginning Thursday afternoon into the late Thursday night. More than 80 million people were under alerts Wednesday as the National Weather Service warned of powerful wind gusts, potentially as intense as 70 mph, that could impact a massive stretch of the East Coast, from South Carolina up to Massachusetts. In addition to New York, other major cities like Boston, Philadelphia and Washington, D.C., would likely receive chilly rainfall on Thanksgiving, but forecasters expected most metropolitan hubs to be spared from the highest amounts. The weather service did note a flash-flooding threat impacting the Southeast on Wednesday could shift toward New York City by Thursday.Up to 5 inches of rain could fall in other places, especially in southeastern states like Florida and the Carolinas. national.title: US announces new tariffs on host of countries including China
national.summary: The new levies would hit many of America's biggest trading partners, including China and the EU.
national.body:
The US has announced a fresh raft of tariffs as President Donald Trump pushes ahead with his signature trade policy.

The new taxes charged on imports to America are set to hit many of the country's biggest trading partners - China, the European Union and 12 other jurisdictions, including Japan, South Korea and Taiwan.

The White House began investigating the trade practices of other countries in March after the US Supreme Court ruled Trump's previously announced Liberation Day tariffs were illegal .

China is facing the highest tariff rate of up to 40%, followed by Vietnam at up to 35%, with others facing either 20% or 25%.

The US Trade Representative (USTR) announced the proposed tariffs together with extensive reports of how each jurisdiction's trade practices purportedly impact American commerce.

The new duties are not expected to take effect until next year and have to go through rounds of public consultation and, potentially, hearings.

Tariffs are taxes levied on imported goods. The amount is typically calculated as a percentage of a good's value and paid to the government by businesses importing products.

Some of these rates will be effectively reduced because of caps on tariffs Trump has agreed to. Individual countries also face different levies.

national.title: Judge temporarily blocks FCC from reviewing ABC's licenses
national.summary: A federal judge blocked the FCC from moving forward with an early review of ABC's broadcast licenses, a move the network argues is an attempt by the Trump administration to punish speech it does not like.
national.body: A federal judge blocked the Federal Communications Commission from moving forward with an early review of ABC's broadcast licenses Wednesday, a move the network argues is an attempt by the Trump administration to punish speech it does not like.In a 45-page ruling, U.S. District Judge Loren AliKhan found ABC is likely to succeed in showing the FCC's license review was retaliatory. Her preliminary injunction bars the FCC from "taking any continuing or further action against [ABC] in relation to the early license renewal proceedings" while the network's lawsuit against the agency works its way through the courts. The judge pointed to at least 11 different examples of President Trump publicly urging the FCC to strip ABC of its licenses in recent years — an action the president argues is necessary because the network's news coverage or late-night shows are unfair to him. AliKhan also said FCC Chair Brendan Carr — who frequently echoes Mr. Trump's criticism of media outlets — "has taken President Trump's rhetoric as his marching orders.""Given the extreme, indeed existential, nature of the possible penalty Plaintiffs face—loss of their broadcast licenses—the court concludes that early license renewal proceedings create a risk sufficient to chill a broadcaster of ordinary firmness," the judge wrote.She said the question of whether ABC's interest in a preliminary injunction outweighed the federal government's interests was "not a close case." She did not agree to ABC's request for a broader ban on "taking any actions, formal or informal, to coerce or threaten Plaintiffs with sanctions in an effort to alter their exercise of editorial discretion."An ABC News spokesperson said: "Today's decision is an important victory for the First Amendment. We thank the court for its careful consideration."An FCC spokesperson called the decision to grant ABC's motion "wrong on the facts and wrong on the law—as controlling Supreme Court precedent makes clear," and said the agency "looks forward to prevailing in full on this matter."Earlier this year, the FCC ordered ABC to file early license renewal applications for the eight local television stations it owns and operates, saying it was investigating "possible violations" of the Communications Act of 1934 and the agency's prohibition on unlawful discrimination. The licenses originally weren't scheduled for renewal until 2028 to 2031

national.title: As foreign troops withdraw from Somalia, could al-Shabab take over?
national.summary: Somalia relies heavily on foreign funding and military support for its very survival.
national.body:
Somalia is facing a fresh test of its stability as foreign troops begin withdrawing, funding for its security forces comes under pressure and a bitter political dispute threatens to derail plans for the country's first direct democratic elections in decades.

The combination of challenges has raised questions about whether the government can defend itself against Islamist militant group al-Shabab while managing growing divisions among political factions.

Some analysts fear the situation could embolden al-Shabab, which is affiliated with al-Qaeda, and potentially allow it to seize control of the capital, Mogadishu.

The group already controls large parts of the country despite the presence of about 12,000 African Union (AU) troops supporting the government.

The withdrawal of foreign forces, alongside the activities of clan-based militias aligned with rival political factions, has heightened concerns about the government's ability to maintain control.

Ugandan troops, who make up the largest contingent of the AU force, began withdrawing last month, with the country expected to complete its withdrawal by next year.

Ethiopia, another major contributor to the AU mission, is also reportedly planning to withdraw about 3,000 troops. The country has 2,500 troops authorised under the AU mission and roughly 5,000 under a bilateral agreement with Somalia. It is not clear whether the reported withdrawals would be from the AU contingent, the bilateral force, or both.

The US, which had earlier announced cuts to funding for the UN Support Office in Somalia (UNSOS) has since said it is extending it for a year. Washington contributes about a quarter of $500m UNSOS's annual budget, which supports Somali security forces, AU missions and individual troop-contributing nations.

national.body: For the first time in history, the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade has been postponed due to weather, Macy's said Wednesday. The 100th annual parade will now kick off Saturday at 8:30 a.m.The historic move comes as a powerful coastal storm is set to impact the area Thursday. "The safety of our participants and spectators is our top priority, and after close consultation with our city and agency partners, we've made the decision to move the celebration due to expected severe weather," Macy's said in a statement. "Thank you to the thousands of volunteers, performers and partners who create the magic millions enjoy each year. We look forward to celebrating together on Saturday.""Created by Macy's colleagues since 1924 as a gift to our city and nation, our parade has brought magic into the hearts of millions and have created cherished memories that have spanned generations," Will Coss, executive producer and vice president of Macy's Branded Entertainment, said at a press conference Wednesday. "This year we marked our 100th march, a milestone built on creativity, celebration and tradition. While we are heartbroken that our parade was postponed, the safety of our participants and spectators is and always will be our top priority." "We know that our city is the greatest city in the world, and we also know that in our city, nothing comes easily, and you have to plan for every possibility," New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said. "And while we were looking forward to celebrating Macy's 100th Thanksgiving Day Parade tomorrow, extreme weather has forced us to reschedule for Saturday instead." Mamdani pointed to the "heavy storm" expected Thursday, with wind gusts up to 65 mph possible, along with potential flash flooding. "Now I know many New Yorkers, myself included as well as millions around the world, were looking forward to the parade being held tomorrow," Mamdani said. "I know that this change of plan will cause inconveniences, yet safety has to come first. And on Saturday, when balloons climb into the sky, every New Yorker and everyone visiting, will be able to take in a show that is both truly spectacular and also safe." national.title: California warns of flooding as King Tides peak over Thanksgiving
national.summary: Parts of the Canadian province of British Columbia may also be affected by the storms and flooding, which come as millions of people travel for the holiday.
national.body:
Coastal areas of California are bracing for potential flooding as king tides peak in the state during the US Thanksgiving holiday.

Water levels across the US state's vast coastline could reach over 8ft (2.4 metres) in some areas on Wednesday and Thursday, according to the National Weather Service (NWS) - breaking records set just last month.

The NWS has warned parts of California could face major coastal flooding, which is likely to be significant in low-lying areas. There have already been some reports of flooding.

Meanwhile, storms are also forecast for the Pacific Northwest, including the Canadian province of British Columbia, and eastern parts of the US.

Portions of a pier in northern California came crashing down into the ocean on Wednesday as high tides and strong waves battered the structure, video showed.

Beachgoers have been advised to stay away from the water's edge as large waves could suddenly form. Such waves could be damaging to piers and jetties, and could capsize small vessels, the NWS warned.

Flooding has already been reported in the San Francisco Bay Area.

In San Diego, a high tide of 8 ft 11in was recorded on Wednesday morning local time - potentially breaking the record for highest tide measured in the area, which was just set late last month at 7.98ft.

national.summary: A federal judge has sided against Democrats on the federal government's taxpayer-funded political ads, which critics say were illegal propaganda intended to promote President Trump.
national.body: A federal judge on Wednesday sided against Democrats on the federal government's taxpayer-funded ads that promoted partisan messages and President Trump ahead of the midterm elections, declining to extend a temporary ban on the ads.U.S. District Judge Loren AliKhan in Washington, D.C., said the Democratic National Committee hadn't shown a likelihood of prevailing in the case. Democrats had argued the TV spots were illegal government-sponsored propaganda intended to promote the president's campaign message just weeks before November's midterm elections. In her ruling, she noted that a previous temporary restraining order against the ads had been issued when the election was less than a week away."But the November 2026 midterm elections have come and gone," she wrote, adding that the DNC was now claiming the party could be harmed by the ads in December congressional runoff elections or even because the 2028 presidential cycle has already begun."At this juncture and on this record, the court is unpersuaded," AliKhan wrote.Her ruling comes after another judge in a similar case in New York also declined a long-term ban on the ads.The ads first emerged on cable and broadcast networks — including CBS — in late September, just over a month before the midterms, funded by a $20 million Department of Homeland Security contract. Many of the ads touted Mr. Trump or his administration's accomplishments, and included the disclosure: "Paid for by the U.S. Government."Members of both parties raised questions about the ads, and Democrats sued the Trump administration in October.The White House has defended the ads as public service announcements akin to what past administrations have made to promote various policies, arguing they are not political ads because they don't explicitly call on viewers to take any particular action. national.title: At least 31 killed after fuel tanker crashes and catches fire near Cairo
national.summary: A crash involving a fuel tanker has ignited a massive fire on a major highway surrounding Cairo, killing at least 31 people.
national.body: A crash involving a fuel tanker ignited a massive fire on a major highway surrounding Cairo on Wednesday, killing at least 31 people, Egyptian authorities said. The blaze on Ring Road, a key artery that encircles the Egyptian capital, also injured at least 21 people and left more than two dozen cars and motorcycles charred, according to the latest figures released by the Health Ministry. The stretch of the highway where the crash occurred was in Warraq, a densely populated neighborhood in Giza, part of the Greater Cairo area, according to the Health Ministry.At the scene, rescue workers were pulling people out of burning cars. An Associated Press video shows firefighters working to put out the fire spreading among the cars. Hundreds of people gathered near the scene in the Warraq district of Imbaba, a Cairo suburb.Ahmed Sameer, who was stuck in traffic as the road was blocked after the accident, saw the fuel truck and many cars on fire. He said he saw at least eight bodies being removed from burned cars."It was a huge fire; the cars got stuck together because of the fire," he told the AP, describing the fear and panic that followed. "It was a shocking scene."Egyptian President Abdel-Fattah el-Sisi expressed his condolences to the victims in a statement. The Public Prosecutor's office said DNA investigations were underway to identify the victims.Health Minister Khaled Abdel Ghaffar said the injured were taken to nearby hospitals and that he would head to the scene himself. He said the death toll was preliminary, raising concerns it could rise further. Initial statements said 25 people were injured, but that figure was later revised to 21.Deadly traffic accidents claim thousands of lives every year in Egypt, which has a poor transportation safety record. Speeding, bad roads and poor enforcement of traffic laws are the main reasons behind most of the crashes.In January, 21 people were killed and 16 were injured in a massive multicar pileup on a road near the southern province of Beni Suef.

national.summary: The U.S. Army detonated a stockpile of degrading explosives at a munitions plant in Iowa on Wednesday, after days of back-and-forth between politicians and the courts.
national.body: The U.S. Army detonated a stockpile of degrading explosives at a munitions plant in Iowa on Wednesday morning, following community outcry and a legal fight over concerns of a possible dust plume containing toxic lead particles spreading after the blast.Five tons of unstable explosive material, containing the highly sensitive compound lead azide, were blown up in a controlled detonation at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, which is a small community of about 350 people, located four hours west of Chicago by car. As scheduled, the detonation took place at 9 a.m. local time. A few loud pops rang out in livestream footage of the explosion published by The Associated Press, followed by a faint smoke cloud that rose up above the rooftop of the Armed Forces Reserve Center building that separated its cameras from the detonation site.Fifteen minutes after it happened, the Environmental Protection Agency reported that zero lead was detected in the air by four monitoring stations in the area. Those sensors continued to show the same readings two hours later, according to the EPA. The Army said in a follow-up social media post Wednesday evening that the Federal Emergency Management Agency had given an "all clear" around the plant. The Army also added that maps from the Pentagon's Defense Threat Reduction Agency indicated "ZERO airborne lead detection" from the detonation. FEMA said in a separate statement Wednesday night that its air monitoring results indicated there was "no detectable lead."Army Maj. Gen. Eric P. Shirley, the commander of the operation, described the detonation as "tremendously successful" at a news conference Wednesday."I believe absolutely that we reduced, as close to zero as is absolutely humanly possible, the risk to the health and the safety of the people of Middletown and the extended communities throughout Iowa," he said.Rob Cekada, the director of the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives, added that the operation went "100% as planned," with the blast driving the explosion into the ground and minimizing the amount of lead dispersed into the atmosphere, as designed. national.title: Andy Taylor, longtime Duran Duran guitarist, dies at 65
national.summary: Andy Taylor, the original guitarist of the 1980s English new wave band Duran Duran, has died at age 65 following a battle with prostate cancer.
national.body: Andy Taylor, the original guitarist of the 1980s English new wave band Duran Duran — whose huge pop hits included "Hungry Like the Wolf," "The Reflex" and "Rio" — and who were inextricably linked to the launch of MTV, has died. He was 65.Taylor died following a "courageous battle with prostate cancer," his family and the band said in a joint statement posted to social media. He died Monday at his home surrounded by friends and family."To the world, Andy was a brilliant guitarist, but to us, he was the most wonderful husband, a loving dad and the proudest grandfather," his family said. On the night he was inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in November 2022, Taylor revealed that he had been battling Stage 4 metastatic prostate cancer for several years and was unable to attend."I would like to thank each of my brothers in this great band," he wrote at the time. "You can dream about what happened to us but to experience it, on one's own terms, as mates, was beyond incredible."His family said Wednesday that Taylor "faced the last few years with so much courage and determination until the very end, never losing his love of life."The two-time Grammy Award winners had nine gold records and six platinum ones, with 20 Top 20 singles in the U.K. and 18 in the U.S. They were two-time Ivor Novello Award winners and are MTV Video Visionary Award recipients."Andy was there at the very beginning of our story," the band said in Wednesday's statement. "From the moment he arrived in Birmingham from the North East with a guitar and an unshakeable belief in what we could become, he brought an indelible fire and swagger to our music."The band's 1981 debut album "Duran Duran" had their first hit single, "Planet Earth," but it was "Rio" that transformed them into trans-Atlantic stars. The Rock Hall explained their appeal this way: "They were new wave outsiders who became music video stars — 'Tiger Beat' fashion pinups who rocked arenas."The band's imperial stage occurred with a trio of hit albums between 1981 and 1983, with such dance-floor barnburners as "Girls on Film" and "Union of the Snake" and the moody ballads "The Chauffeur" and "Save a Prayer." national.title: The US pastor who wants to see women's right to vote overturned
national.summary: The movement to repeal women's right to vote has gained traction amongst some very conservative Christians.
national.body:
"Patriarchy is in accordance with the way God made the world." That is the view of Pastor Doug Wilson, a conservative minister who the US Secretary of Defence Pete Hegseth calls his mentor.

Speaking to the BBC from his base in Moscow, Idaho, Wilson explained his view that a society led by men is "a very great blessing". It's a perspective Christians who disagree with him say is based on a fundamentalist understanding of the Bible, which promotes the subjugation of women.

A self-described Christian nationalist, Wilson believes the US should be a theocracy, with gay sex criminalised, abortion outlawed, and people of other faiths unable to hold public office.

In the past he has delivered a sermon on "The Lost Virtue of Sexism," arguing that the Bible says women should be excluded from leadership of the church, and certain roles in civic affairs. And as part of his views on the division between the sexes, he would like the 19th Amendment of the US constitution, which granted women the right to vote, to be repealed, something his detractors say is anti-democratic.

The vast majority of Christians support women's right to vote, and dismiss his message as misogynistic and extreme.

Rev. Canon Dana Colley Corsello, the vicar at the Washington National Cathedral, rejects Wilson's understanding of what the Bible says about women's roles.

"In my mind, there is no biblical precedent or standing for what [Wilson has] proposed," she told the BBC.

"I'm married, I have a husband, I have children. My husband and I are complete equals in everything we do."

national.title: US Army says controlled blast of explosives in Iowa was 'huge success'
national.summary: Despite widespread concern from residents ahead of the blast, officials say that lead readings in the area so far have been promising.
national.body:
The US military has hailed as a "huge success" the detonation of nearly five tonnes of toxic explosives in Iowa, an operation that sparked fears of health and environmental problems across the region.

Smoke was seen rising into the sky shortly after 09:00 local time (14:00 GMT) following the explosion, as the Army declared the risk "as close to zero as is absolutely humanly possible".

Plans to detonate the lead azide, a volatile compound reportedly at risk of exploding on its own, were paused several times before the blast following public outcry and legal challenges.

On Wednesday evening, the Army said that an "all clear" has been issued around the ammunition plant.

President Donald Trump said shortly after the blast that reports showed mitigation efforts "far exceeded expectations".

"The Army's controlled, mitigated detonation exceeded all expectations and was a HUGE success," Adam Telle, acting secretary of the US Army, wrote on social media.

Despite widespread concern from residents of Middletown, Iowa, ahead of the blast, officials have said that lead readings in the area so far have been promising.

In a Wednesday evening update on X, the Army said that the Federal Emergency Management Agency (Fema) had issued the "all clear" around the plant and that there was no airborne lead detection following the detonation.

Plans to detonate the lead azide, a volatile compound reportedly at risk of exploding on its own, were paused several times before the blast following public outcry and legal challenges.

On Wednesday evening, the Army said that an "all clear" has been issued around the ammunition plant.

President Donald Trump said shortly after the blast that reports showed mitigation efforts "far exceeded expectations".

"The Army's controlled, mitigated detonation exceeded all expectations and was a HUGE success," Adam Telle, acting secretary of the US Army, wrote on social media.

Despite widespread concern from residents of Middletown, Iowa, ahead of the blast, officials have said that lead readings in the area so far have been promising.

In a Wednesday evening update on X, the Army said that the Federal Emergency Management Agency (Fema) had issued the "all clear" around the plant and that there was no airborne lead detection following the detonation.

national.title: Spanish elections: What you need to know and what's at stake
national.summary: After eight years of Socialist-led rule, snap elections are taking place on Sunday with conservative Alberto Núñez Feijóo vying to win office.
national.body:
After eight years of Socialist-led government under Pedro Sánchez, Spain is at a crossroads.

Snap elections are taking place on Sunday 29 November, and voters face a choice of continued left-wing rule or a conservative-led government, with the likely support of far-right Vox.

Alberto Núñez Feijóo's conservative People's Party is narrowly ahead of the Socialist PSOE in most polls.

He has spoken of Spain being probably at "the most significant moment in our country for the past 50 years", and he aims to "repair the state, regenerate democracy, reunited the nation and recover Spain's ambition and self-esteem". But it is unlikely he could do anything without the backing of Vox, who are third in the opinion polls.

For more on Feijóo and who else to watch in this election - read here .

Spain has a population of almost 50 million, and almost 39 million people have the right to vote for the Congress and the upper house, the Senate. The polls open at 09:00 (08:00 GMT) on Sunday and close at 20:00 (19:00 GMT), when the first exit polls come out.

Sánchez called this vote eight months early after MPs rejected planned changes to Spain's housing laws.

He was responding to nationwide protests after an 87-year-old woman called Maricarmen Abascal was evicted from her rented flat in Madrid and later died.

national.title: France's political mainstream risks presidential vote debacle with no clear candidate
national.summary: Hard-right and hard-left candidates dominate the polls ahead of next year's presidential election.
national.body:
France's political mainstream faces wipe-out at the presidential election in April-May 2027, unless it acts fast to choose who it wishes to stand.

With every poll confirming the dominance of hard-right and hard-left leaders Marine Le Pen and Jean-Luc Mélenchon, candidates of the middle-ground – the old "legacy" parties – are being squeezed out of the game.

In theory any contender from centre-right or centre-left who was chosen in the first multi-candidate round of voting in April should be in a strong position to win in the play-off a fortnight later.

That is because at their separate ends of the spectrum both Le Pen and Mélenchon have more people who oppose than support them.

But personal rivalries, lack of preparation and differing political visions have so far put paid to any hope of a meaningful challenge.

"The game in the centre is totally blocked," says political writer François Fressoz at the left-leaning Le Monde newspaper. "The partisans of reason have lost their reason."

On the left – the old Socialist Party and its acolytes – there is at least agreement on a candidate: European Parliament MP Raphaël Glucksmann.

His problem is that allies who he might once have counted on – Greens, Communists and other small left-wing parties, not to mention many Socialist voters – are being pulled inexorably into the Mélenchon orbit.

national.title: Has global jihadism failed, or is it simply changing shape?
national.summary: Jihadist groups appear to be focusing on local issues rather than global terror. Does it signify a real change?
national.body:
Rice, pasta, sugar, cooking oil and beans are hardly what you'd expect to see in jihadist propaganda. Yet these were among the supplies that al-Qaeda's Somali branch, al-Shabab, said its "charity" had handed out to hundreds of struggling families in August, as it publicised the aid through its social media accounts and radio station.

The group, which controls large parts of rural southern and central Somalia, has been keen to show off its so-called humanitarian work throughout 2026.

"May God reward them," said a local woman in one of al-Shabab's videos.

It's all part of an effort to win over local communities and present itself as more than just a jihadist group.

A quarter of a century after al-Qaeda's 9/11 attacks in the US, and 12 years after Islamic State group (IS) declared its so-called caliphate in Iraq and Syria, the jihadist movement looks very different.

Rather than focusing on attacking the West or fighting for a global Islamic state, some - especially those linked to al-Qaeda - are putting more effort into winning power closer to home. And they seem increasingly willing to make compromises along the way.

Because of this, a debate is growing within the movement. While hardliners reject compromise, pragmatists see working with local groups and former enemies as a way to gain power. But do the pragmatists represent a genuine change or simply a shift in tactics to achieve the same ultimate goals: establishing a state that applies their strict interpretation of Islamic Sharia law both at home and in its dealings with the outside world?

Neither al-Qaeda nor IS has achieved its ultimate dream: taking over one or more countries and ruling them according to their strict interpretation of Islam.

national.title: US approves SpaceX plan to send a million data satellites to space
national.summary: The Starmind constellation aims to be the most cost and energy-efficient way to meet the growing demand for AI computing power.
national.body:
US regulators have given SpaceX the go-ahead to launch a million satellites into Earth's orbit to help build data centres in space - the first approval of its kind.

The company, which is owned by Elon Musk, wants to use sunlight to power satellites that will process data for AI and send the results back to Earth.

The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) said on Wednesday that the project, known as Starmind, will "support America's booming super intelligence economy".

Its approval comes as communities across the US have pushed back against the expansion of data centres on the ground.

Space X believes the "orbital data centres" are the most cost and energy-efficient way to meet the growing demand for artificial intelligence (AI) computing power that is beyond "terrestrial capabilities".

FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said in a statement that the project "opens a bold new frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America's leadership and growth".

"This is the kind of American ingenuity that can unite our strengths in space and advanced technology, reinforce our economic leadership, and expand prosperity here at home," Carr said.

Responding to the announcement, Musk wrote on X: "Much appreciated. This will be a great asset to America and the world."

national.title: Small plane crash off Mississippi coast kills extended family of 6 on fishing trip
national.summary: Authorities are investigating why a small plane carrying six members of a Florida family crashed off the Mississippi coast on Tuesday. They were returning home from a fishing trip, relatives say.
national.body:
Gene Johnson, Associated Press Gene Johnson, Associated Press

Authorities are investigating why a small plane carrying six members of a Florida family crashed off the Mississippi coast on Tuesday. They were returning home from a fishing trip, relatives say.

The plane's pilot was Brent Stokes, the 50-year-old president of a marine contracting company based in Fort Myers, according to Jackson County Coroner Bruce Lynd Jr. Stokes' company's website described him as an "avid fisherman and life time boater."

The other victims were Stokes' 16-year-old son, Hunter Stokes; Stokes' sister, Arlyn Knox, 43; her husband, Michael Knox, 43; and their two sons, 12-year-old Charles Holden Knox and 10-year-old Truett Knox.

Arlyn and Michael Knox ran Knox Technologies, a Fort Myers-based IT company they founded in 2012, according to the company's website.

The Knox and Stokes families confirmed their deaths in an emailed statement provided to The Associated Press.

"They died doing what they loved: celebrating the start of a wonderful holiday season with a fishing trip together, before heading home to be with the rest of our family," the statement said. "In the middle of our grief, we are holding on to that, and to how much love they gave us and how much love surrounds us now. We will carry them with us always."

Lynd said that autopsies are being performed on Brent Stokes and Michael Knox, who was also a licensed pilot.

national.title: Macy's postpones Thanksgiving parade due to weather
national.summary: The was the first time ever that the iconic celebration - known for its massive balloons floating past the city's skyscrapers - was delayed because of storms.
national.body:
Macy's has postponed its 100th annual Thanksgiving Day Parade in New York to Saturday because of severe weather.

Preparations to hold the iconic holiday celebration, known for its massive balloons that float among the city's skyscrapers, had already begun when the forecast for heavy rain and strong winds on Thursday led to the delay.

The last time the parade was suspended was during World War Two, but it has never been postponed due to weather. In 1971, Macy's decided to ground the balloons, which often feature beloved characters from pop culture, because of weather.

A powerful coastal storm is set to affect the New York area in coming days.

The potent nor'easter storm is expected to make it too windy and dangerous for the iconic balloons to fly.

Macy's had expected to put 100 inflatables into the sky to mark its 100th parade and feature 10 new balloons, including one depicting the animated dog Bluey wearing a crown and another showing a Minion character riding a banana like a horse.

"While we are heartbroken that our parade was postponed, the safety of our partners, the safety of our participants and spectators is, and always will be, our top priority," said Will Cross, the parade's executive producer, during a news conference on Wednesday with city officials.

Cross also said the giant balloons would be deflated on Wednesday night and stored at a facility in neighbouring New Jersey until they were reinflated for the parade on Saturday.

national.summary: Vice President JD Vance, second lady Usha Vance and their four children visited Wright-Patterson Air Force Base in Ohio on Wednesday, serving a Thanksgiving meal to troops and joining them for lunch.

WRIGHT-PATTERSON AIR FORCE BASE, Ohio (AP) — Vice President JD Vance, second lady Usha Vance and their four children visited Wright-Patterson Air Force Base in Ohio on Wednesday, serving a Thanksgiving meal to troops and joining them for lunch in what Vance called an "amazing opportunity" to have "unfiltered, off-the-record" conversations with service members.

The family is spending the holiday in the state, and the base in southwest Ohio is about 60 miles (97 kilometers) from their home in Cincinnati and close to where Vance was born. In tow for the trip: Ewan, 9; Vivek, 6; Mirabel, 4; and four-month-old Alec.

WATCH: Army carries out controlled detonation of Iowa lead azide stockpile amid concerns

Along a cafeteria-style food line, Vance asked civilians and uniformed active-duty service members for their home state and whether they wanted roast turkey, prime rib or baked ham. The Republican vice president then passed plates along to his son Ewan, who spooned out sides including sweet potatoes, green beans, cornbread, corn calico and mashed potatoes.

"Ewan, this is an Ohioan, you want to ask?" Vance asked his son, whom he called a "dedicated Ohio sports fan." Ewan then quizzed the man about his status as an Ohio State fan.

"Better a Bulldogs fan than the Buckeyes this year," the vice president told one man who said he was from Georgia, whose football team has been highly ranked all season.

Usha Vance, with baby Alec in her arms and Mirabel nearby, chatted with attendees as they waited in line.

national.summary: A year after one of Hong Kong's deadliest fires, families left behind are still waiting for justice.
national.body:
It was a sunny Wednesday afternoon on 26 November last year, and Mrs Lau was attending a dance class at an activity centre close to her home.

At around 14:45 she heard the faint sounds of fire engine sirens - but didn't think much of it.

It was only a while later, when she started receiving calls from a friend, that she found out that Wang Fuk Court - the eight-block apartment complex she had called home for the past 40 years - was ablaze. And her husband - a wheelchair user - was trapped inside their home.

"I grabbed my things quickly and ran down without even putting my shoes on properly," Mrs Lau, who wanted to be identified only by her surname, told the BBC.

When she got there, the building had been cordoned off by police.

She called her 74-year-old husband but he told her not to worry - he hadn't heard an alarm so it was probably a small fire, he said.

Mrs Lau could only watch helplessly as the blaze tore through Wang Fuk Court at a peak speed of about 10m (33ft) per second - an "unprecedented" rate, a final report released by an independent committee in relation to the deadly blaze that killed 168 people found.

It was a tragedy that was entirely preventable but happened as a result of a series of human errors, fire safety failures, alleged fraud and suspected corruption, said the report.

national.title: Angelina Jolie and Brad Pitt settle legal battle over French winery
national.summary: The Hollywood A-listers' legal battle focused on the vineyard they bought in 2008 and where they wed six years later.
national.body:
Brad Pitt and Angelina Jolie have settled a long-running legal battle over her sale of a stake in their French vineyard, which unfolded amid a bitter divorce.

"We have settled out of court in the best interests of our family and will not be commenting further," said the Hollywood stars' representatives in a joint statement.

They bought a controlling interest in Château Miraval in 2008 and wed there six years later.

In the lawsuit, Pitt , 62, argued that Jolie , 51, acted without his permission in selling her share in the winery to a Russian oligarch. She counter-sued, accusing Pitt of drunkenly attacking her and their children on a flight, prompting her to file for divorce in 2016.

The settlement announced on Wednesday resolves both of their respective legal actions.

"Any comments in media stories attributed to 'sources' are in fact not coming from either of us, or anyone close to us," said the statement from their representatives.

Pitt's lawsuit had accused Jolie of seeking "to inflict harm" on him when she sold her stake in their co-owned vineyard, which he claimed had forced him to partner with "a stranger with poisonous associations and intentions".

The Fight Club star said he and Jolie had agreed not to sell their stakes in the venue without the permission of the other.

national.title: Alaska ends voter data agreement with Justice Department, which had been searching for noncitizens
national.summary: A Republican official who oversees Alaska elections said she has ended an agreement under which the state shared its voter registration list with the U.S. Department of Justice and allowed the agency to flag voters for possible removal.
national.body:
Becky Bohrer, Associated Press Becky Bohrer, Associated Press

JUNEAU, Alaska (AP) — A Republican official who oversees Alaska elections said she has ended an agreement under which the state shared its voter registration list with the U.S. Department of Justice and allowed the agency to flag voters for possible removal.

No voters were removed as a result of the agreement signed last December, and the Justice Department since then had not identified "any potentially ineligible voters or raised concerns regarding Alaska's voter registration records," the office of outgoing Lt. Gov. Nancy Dahlstrom said.

Dahlstrom said she notified the Justice Department that Alaska was terminating the agreement, effective Monday. That's also when Alaska officials announced that the results of the Nov. 3 general election, in which Democrats flipped a U.S. Senate seat and the governor's office, had been certified.

The Alaska Division of Elections directed the department to destroy the confidential voter information the state provided, Dahlstrom's office said in a statement released late Monday. A Justice Department spokesperson on Tuesday said the agency would send a formal response to the state.

The federal government's demand for detailed state voter information was part of a broader effort throughout the midterm election cycle to promote the idea that scores of noncitizens were on state voter rolls and potentially casting ballots illegally. In fact, years of research, state investigations and the Justice Department's own record of arrests showed the issue to be extremely rare.

The Justice Department sued 30 states and the District of Columbia for not complying with its demands to provide detailed voter registration data or other election-related records, with 28 of those lawsuits dismissed by courts, according to the Brennan Center for Justice. The department entered a settlement agreement with Oklahoma and dismissed its case with that state, the group said.

Alaska was one of at least 16 states to provide voter lists that included information such as driver's license and partial Social Security numbers, dates of birth and addresses. Alaska and Texas also signed data-sharing agreements with the Justice Department, in which it outlined plans for its own analysis of voter files, its plans to flag voter list issues and directions for removing voters deemed ineligible.

national.title: Georgia's Fulton County ordered to give copy of 2020 election records seized by FBI to state board
national.summary: A judge on Tuesday ordered Georgia's Fulton County to turn over a digital copy of ballots and other election records seized by the FBI earlier this year to the State Election Board, which had been trying for more than two years to obtain certain records from the 2020 election in the state's most pop
national.body:
Kate Brumback, Associated Press Kate Brumback, Associated Press

ATLANTA (AP) — A judge on Tuesday ordered Georgia's Fulton County to turn over a digital copy of ballots and other election records seized by the FBI earlier this year to the State Election Board, which had been trying for more than two years to obtain certain records from the 2020 election in the state's most populous county.

Fulton County Superior Court Judge Kelly Lee Ellerbe ordered that the records be delivered to the state board by 5 p.m. Wednesday. She also put in place a protective order that limits who can see the unredacted records.

A Fulton County spokesperson declined to comment on a pending legal matter. The State Election Board did not immediately respond to an email seeking comment.

The FBI served a search warrant at the Fulton County elections hub on Jan. 28 seeking records related to the 2020 election, leaving with hundreds of boxes containing ballots and other records. The county unsuccessfully sought to have a judge order the return of the records, but the federal government did provide the county with what it said was a digital copy of the records that were taken.

The overwhelmingly Democratic county, which includes most of the city of Atlanta, has been a target of President Donald Trump and his allies since he narrowly lost the presidential election in Georgia to Democrat Joe Biden in 2020. Trump has consistently insisted without evidence that widespread voter fraud in the county cost him victory in the state. Multiple courts and state and federal officials have found no evidence of fraud that would have altered the outcome.

A statement from an FBI agent supporting the search warrant used to take the records said the agency was examining possible "deficiencies or defects" in Fulton County's 2020 vote count. More than six years after that election and 10 months after the records seizure, no charges have been filed.

The FBI in July instructed field offices across the country to dedicate more than 200 staffers to its investigation of the 2020 election in Fulton County, describing it as a "priority investigation," and The New York Times reported that the FBI and federal prosecutors last week interviewed the man who served as the county's election director in 2020.

national.summary: Kilmar Ábrego García, a Salvadoran national who fought his mistaken deportation from the United States, arrived in Spain on Wednesday after what his lawyer described as a temporary departure, with hopes of returning to his family's home in Maryland after President Donald Trump leaves office.
national.body:
Suman Naishadham, Associated Press Suman Naishadham, Associated Press

Michael Kunzelman, Associated Press Michael Kunzelman, Associated Press

MADRID (AP) — Kilmar Ábrego García, a Salvadoran national who fought his mistaken deportation from the United States, arrived in Spain on Wednesday after what his lawyer described as a temporary departure, with hopes of returning to his family's home in Maryland after President Donald Trump leaves office.

Ábrego García, who has an American wife and child, was arrested in Baltimore in March 2025 and was deported to a Salvadoran prison in what an official called an "administrative error." A judge later ordered his return to the U.S., where he fought the Trump administration's efforts to deport him again, this time to Africa.

After receiving officials' permission to leave the U.S., Ábrego García voluntarily departed on Tuesday from Washington Dulles International Airport, accompanied by his wife.

"The government does not decide where my story continues," the 31-year-old said during a virtual news conference Wednesday after he arrived in Spain. "My family and I will decide our future."

Simon Sandoval-Moshenberg, a Virginia-based attorney representing Ábrego García, called the move "a temporary departure," though he declined to say what his client's immediate plans are, including where he will live.

"Mr. Ábrego García has many options to return to the United States as the husband of a U.S. citizen spouse and the father of a U.S. citizen child. We don't expect that to happen under this administration, which we know will never give him a fair shake, but we expect that the next administration will prioritize reunifying this family and bringing him back to Maryland," Sandoval-Moshenberg said.

national.title: Thirty-one killed in massive fire as fuel tanker crashes on Cairo highway
national.summary: Another 21 are injured after the tanker reportedly overturns on a busy ring road in the Egyptian capital.
national.body:
Thirty-one people have been killed and 21 others injured in a large fire on a busy highway in Cairo after a fuel tanker crashed, Egypt's health ministry says.

Hospitals nearby treated patients suffering burns and smoke inhalation after the incident, which occurred on a section of a ring road in the Warraq neighbourhood, to the north of the old city centre, on Wednesday evening.

Footage circulating on social media showed billowing flames and black smoke towering high into the night sky, with multiple nearby vehicles torched.

Officials have not given an account of how the fire broke out, but state-owned media reported the tanker had overturned, dousing nearby vehicles with petrol.

The regional public prosecutor has launched an investigation into the incident and asked that DNA samples be taken from bodies of the dead.

The tanker, which belonged to a private contractor, had been travelling along the highway when a high-voltage cable fell in front of it, prompting the driver to lose control, Al-Ahram reports, citing sources with knowledge of the investigation.

It then crossed the central reservation, overturned and caught fire, the state-owned newspaper says.

Egypt has suffered several deadly fires in recent years, with informal residential areas and often run-down infrastructure making incidents more common, the response to which is often complicated by slow emergency response times and locally improvised rescue efforts, even in the sprawling Egyptian capital.

national.title: These young Republicans have a message for their party: It's time to 'grow up'
national.summary: Three weeks after midterm elections that devastated the Republican Party, several dozen of its more youthful members gathered at a brewery to sort through the pieces.
national.body:
Jesse Bedayn, Associated Press Jesse Bedayn, Associated Press

FORT WORTH, Texas (AP) — Three weeks after midterm elections that devastated the Republican Party, several dozen of its more youthful members gathered at a brewery to sort through the pieces.

The Monday meeting was organized by the Tarrant County Young Republicans, a local organization on the front lines of a national reckoning. Their last leader resigned shortly before the midterms because she couldn't bring herself to vote for some of her party's candidates. Then their county, once a conservative stronghold, flipped blue.

"Everyone has someone to blame, and that finger is never pointed at ourself," said Derrick Wilson, who heads the Texas Young Republican Federation, a coalition that includes the Tarrant County chapter. "So we're going to have to get past that and figure out, what did we do wrong?"

WATCH: How the Latino shift to Democrats helped turn Texas blue

Democrats won the U.S. Senate race and the governor's office in Texas, their first statewide victories in over three decades. There's no consensus about the path forward, but several people at this week's meeting gave similar answers.

Some are bored with "owning the libs" and put off by meme-driven political messaging that they see as flippant in the face of real challenges. Many felt President Donald Trump didn't follow through on his promises. And others gave similar advice to their party leaders: "grow up," "take themselves seriously" and "be humble."

The event opened with someone introduced by Wilson as a "survivor" of the midterms. State Appeals Court Judge Brian Walker, a Republican who won reelection, gave a withering assessment of how the party had stumbled down the wrong path with Trump-style belligerent politics led by the "loudest" and "craziest" voices.

local.body: Another round of proposals to close some Buffalo Public Schools is back on the table — one submitted by the interim schools superintendent and another put forward by some board members.Interim Schools Superintendent Dr. Ebony Prophet-Bullock submitted the district's plan, tweaked from the original that was voted down. It proposes to close the Early Childhood Center, the Bilingual School, Drew Science, Riverside Academy, PS 131 Academy School and East Community High School. However, it no longer includes changes for Middle Early College.“The superintendent's first plan was not a bad plan, just over time, it got really, really muddy up,” stated Erik Bohen, Park District School Board Member.“We have to make sure we do this right and do it well.”But four board members submitted their own proposal. Daniel Futures School in the city's Fruit Belt.“The issue is though -- we are running out of money, and we will not have money next year,” declared Bohen.Bohen told me the board could vote Monday night during a special session."I believe 95-percent certain that that will get done," Bohen remarked. “What makes you so confident that it could be done on Monday?” Buckley asked. “Just from my talking's with other board colleagues, I believe no one’s telling me how they're voting but, I believe everybody has their mind made up of where we go, and I believe they've also had pressure from the community as well to get this done," replied Bohen.Both plans still call to phase out Riverside High School.Riverside social studies teacher Marc Bruno told me he doesn't trust the process."This process has been a train wreck from the day it started," Bruno commented. local.body: Small businesses along Buffalo's Elmwood Avenue are gearing up for what they hope will be a big weekend for local shopping.Small Business Saturday is this weekend, serving as a community-driven counterpoint to the retail push of Black Friday.I spoke with several Elmwood Village business owners. Tracey Wei, who owns zero-waste home and body care store Little Salmon, described the area as "welcoming and walkable."Wei told me independent businesses like hers often rely on Small Business Saturday to stay afloat."This weekend is like make-or-break for the last quarter," Wei said.Like many businesses in the neighborhood, she'll be holding a sale on Saturday to promote more foot traffic."Businesses need your money more than billionaires, so every dollar you spend, like 70-80% of it stays with the community," she said.WATCH: 'Make-or-break': Buffalo businesses prepare for Small Business SaturdayOther owners pointed to the unique experience shoppers find in the neighborhood."There are many unique shops you're not gonna find somewhere else, and you get better customer service," Wendie Reed said.At Reed's consignment store, Scoop Shop, shoppers might even find an outfit for the World's Largest Disco on Saturday at the Buffalo Convention Center.Small Business Saturday is one of many events being held to bring people to the area. Seamus Gallivan, the new executive director of the Elmwood Village Association, said the density of the neighborhood is part of its appeal."The beautiful thing about this neighborhood is there are so many businesses so close together that however you get here, you can stay on foot for hours and find everything you need and more," Gallivan explained. He said the stores will also participate in a Christmas window display competition starting December 5. For now, the focus is on bringing people out this Saturday. The day carries real weight for the neighborhood's businesses, said Christa Penner, who owns ShopCraft. "It's a huge day for us, and it's really important that other members of the community come out and support the small businesses in your neighborhoods," Penner said.This story was reported on-air by a journalist and has been converted to this platform with the assistance of AI. local.title: Concerns raised over conditions at cemetery between Colden and Holland

local.body: Overturned headstones, fallen tree limbs and overgrown vegetation are raising concerns about a cemetery between Colden and Holland.Jeffrey Smith contacted me after visiting the cemetery and becoming concerned about what he found. He said the grounds have not been properly maintained, leaving some burial sites partially obscured by vegetation and debris.“Everything when it was green this summer, you couldn't even see part of these stones because the growth was bad,” Smith said. “And now the leaves and limbs are all over the place.”Smith also pointed to a large tree limb that had fallen near burial sites, raising concerns about the potential for additional damage to headstones.“The big limb just came down over there this year apparently,” he said. “This was here in the spring when we came up and checked.”Smith said veterans are among those buried at the cemetery and believes their graves deserve better care.“All these veterans have served our country," he said. "We should be taking care of their graves." WATCH: Concerns raised over conditions at cemetery between Colden and Holland7 News contacted the Town of Colden to figure out who is responsible for maintaining the property. Documents show that the cemetery is privately owned.Town officials said Scouts sometimes volunteer to help clean up the grounds.7 News also contacted the property owner for comment about the cemetery's condition but did not receive a response. Smith lives nearly two hours away and said he cannot regularly visit to monitor the property. He hopes someone will take action.“I'd like to see it cleaned up, maintained, lawn mowed and for it to look proper,” Smith said.He hopes the cemetery can be restored to a condition that is respectful to the people buried there and the families who come to visit.

local.body:
WESTFIELD — A Portland resident is facing charges after he allegedly spray-painted and attempted to drill a hole into the Lincoln statue in the village.

At approximately 2:42 p.m. Wednesday, the Westfield Police Department responded to a criminal mischief complaint at Main and Portage streets. A male wearing a flannel shirt, later identified as Nicholas A. Rychick, was spray-painting and attempting to drill a hole into the bronze statue of Abraham Lincoln. A bystander confronted Rychick, 37, who fled in a vehicle.

With assistance from the Chautauqua County Sheriff's Office and New York State Police, officers located Rychick and his vehicle at a residence in Portland. He was taken into custody without incident and transported to WPD.

The investigation determined that Rychick allegedly attempted to drill a hole into the chest of the memorial to place an arrow into the statue but was unsuccessful. He allegedly proceeded to spray-paint the memorial, damaging it and surrounding holiday decorations.

Rychick was arrested on the above charges, processed and released on appearance tickets directing him to appear before the Town of Westfield Court at a later date.

The Westfield Police Department thanks the concerned citizen who intervened, the Chautauqua County Sheriff's Office and the New York State Police for their assistance.

The statue, which was erected in 1999, showcases unique, bronze statues of Lincoln and Grace Bedell, the girl who suggested that he grow a beard for his presidential campaign.

Grace Bedell, a young girl from Westfield wrote a letter to Mr. Abraham Lincoln, Presidential Candidate, in 1860, encouraging him to “grow whiskers and her brothers would vote for him and he would look nicer.”

local.body: Two fires in the same building destroyed two businesses in North Tonawanda. Now, neighbors are rallying to help the owners.On November 17, an apartment fire damaged Matt Hoffman's Academy Auction House and Carl Cederman's Carl's Tattooing, but optimism was in the air."A lot of water damage, but it wasn't crazy," Hoffman said."We cleaned up," Cederman said. local.title: Brighton preparing for first phase of its Multiversity Trail project
local.summary: The town is focusing on a stretch of the Lehigh Valley Trail that will be part of the network.
local.body:
The town of Brighton has received a $1.4 million grant from the state to improve a section of the Lehigh Valley Trail between the University of Rochester and Rochester Institute of Technology.

The work is part of the town's Multiversity Trail effort that aims to link the university, RIT, and Monroe Community College campuses using the Lehigh Valley Trail and the Erie Canalway Trail. On the Lehigh Valley Trail leg, the town plans to replace most of the surface, among other things.

"It's an old rail trail, the old Lehigh Valley train line, but you know it really needs upgrading, accessibility, signage, drainage issues," Brighton Supervisor Bill Moehle said. "So we'll be able to address all of those and more with this grant."

Moehle added that the town also wants to install flashing beacons at major road crossings that trail users would be able to activate, similar to the Auburn Trail.

Local News Brighton wants to connect bike trails for students at 3 campuses Jeremy Moule The town has three colleges within and along its borders. It wants students at them to be able to easily bike between campuses. The Lehigh Valley Trail work marks the first phase of the Multiversity Trail project. The town plans to put out a request for proposals around design work early next year.

Moehle said the project will benefit more than the college communities. The Lehigh trail is well used, he said, and an important connector for people living on the west side of town.

"It'll focus on the connection between the U of R and RIT because, you know, we have something there to work with," Moehle said. "There is an existing trail, and this will make it really much more user friendly for all users."

local.title: State announces increased road patrols during holiday weekend
local.summary: Motorists heading out for the holiday are being urged to play it safe. On Wednesday, state Gov. Kathy Hochul announced State Police and local law enforcement agencies statewide will increase patrols to target impaired and reckless driving during the Thanksgiving travel season. Funded by the Governor
local.body:
Motorists heading out for the holiday are being urged to play it safe.

On Wednesday, state Gov. Kathy Hochul announced State Police and local law enforcement agencies statewide will increase patrols to target impaired and reckless driving during the Thanksgiving travel season. Funded by the Governor's Traffic Safety Committee (GTSC), the impaired driving enforcement mobilization will run through Sunday.

"As we gather with friends and family to celebrate Thanksgiving, I want to ensure that everyone gets where they are going safely and not have what should be happy memories marred by a preventable tragedy," Hochul said. "I urge drivers to stay alert, stay sober and move over when you see vehicles stopped on the side of the road. If you're in a vehicle, you should wear seat belts or use proper restraint. I thank our law enforcement for sacrificing their time with loved ones to work on Thanksgiving and throughout the holidays to help keep New York's roadways safe."

In addition to increased traffic volume, the Thanksgiving holiday period is also associated with increased alcohol use. During the 2025 Thanksgiving holiday period, law enforcement officers arrested 2,236 drivers for driving while impaired by alcohol or drugs, 12,496 for speeding and also issued 3,075 tickets to unbelted drivers and passengers.

New York State Police Superintendent Steven G. James said, "Our members work vigilantly year-round to keep our roadways safe and prevent the needless tragedies that result from impaired and reckless driving. As always, we will be doing our part to ensure the holidays are safe for all who live in and travel through our great state. Please think twice before getting behind the wheel of a vehicle if you've been drinking. If you have had alcohol, there are several options available that will provide you with a safe ride to your destination. Together, let's make safety a top priority on our roadways this holiday season."

The State Police will supplement regular patrols statewide through efforts including fixed sobriety checkpoints and utilizing Concealed Identity Traffic Enforcement (CITE) patrol vehicles to better spot distracted drivers and those talking or texting on handheld devices. These unmarked vehicles blend in with everyday traffic but are unmistakable as emergency vehicles once the emergency lighting is activated.

Mtorists must follow the state's Move Over law, which was expanded in March 2024 to require drivers to slow down and move over for all vehicles stopped along the roadway if they can safely do so. The Thruway Authority and state Department of Transportation urge motorists to stay alert while driving, slow down and safely move over when they see a vehicle on the side of the road. The lives of motorists, employees, roadway workers and emergency personnel depend on it.

entertainment.title: Late Duran Duran guitarist Andy Taylor shared how music helped him cope with ‘death sentence’ cancer diagnosis
entertainment.summary: The musician died after a battle with cancer.
entertainment.body:
Andy Taylor got candid about how music helped him cope with his Stage 4 metastatic prostate cancer diagnosis years before he died at the age of 65.

“Because I do music … it’s really helped me to live with the pessimism of an incurable disease, but the optimism of making music,” the Duran Duran guitarist shared on a 2023 segment of Channel 5 News .

At the time, he reflected on his 2018 diagnosis, sharing how he was determined to get “the most out of life.”

“I just thought, I’m going to live life,” Taylor continued, explaining he had continued to make music and tour with friends.

“I often say to people, ‘Every minute’s like an hour, every day’s like a week,'” he said. “You really want to get the most out of life.”

Taylor shared that he’s “been very fortunate,” adding, “I’ve had so much in terms of living the dream.”

Elsewhere in the interview, Taylor recalled life shortly before his diagnosis, sharing how he started experiencing symptoms and had “what felt like tumors” on his neck.

“No one could be prepared for that,” he said, recalling when he received the news from the doctor about his condition following a biopsy.

entertainment.title: WWE’s Terri Runnels & Dustin Rhodes Share Death of 3-Year-Old Grandson
entertainment.summary: Terri Runnels and Dustin Rhodes are facing a devastating loss. The former WWE wrestling duo shared that their 3-year-old grandson Rowan has died, although they did not share how the toddler...
entertainment.body:
Terri Runnels and Dustin Rhodes are facing a devastating loss.

The former WWE wrestling duo shared that their 3-year-old grandson Rowan has died, although they did not share how the toddler passed.

Terri confirmed the news on Facebook , sharing a statement for her and Dustin’s daughter Dakota Runnels and her husband Bleau .

“On behalf of Dakota, Bleau, and their families, we share the tragic news of the untimely passing of their sweet beautiful boy, Rowan Dane Oney,” the Nov. 25 post read. “We ask that you respect their privacy at this time. Please no calls or visits. We will post more details soon. Please be in prayer for our family.”

Dustin also asked for prayers for his daughter and her husband, writing in a follow-up message on X, “Guys my grandson Rowan has passed. Please keep us all in your prayers during this time. I am here with @DakotaRunnels22 now.”

The 57-year-old went on to remember the young boy by sharing a photo of himself and Rowan, writing, "Rest in Peace baby boy. I love u so much Rowan."

Terri and Dustin were married from 1993 to 1999. Dustin—the son of WWE Hall of Fame Dusty Rhodes —wrestled for the WWE on and off from 1995 to 2019 under the ring name Goldust . Terri—who was her ex-husband’s manager at the time—joined the WWE under the name Marlena , playing the part of Goldust's cigar-smoking manager.

During her years with the WWE, Terri made sure that she was still able to be there for her daughter, explaining that she told founder Vince McMahon she would not do non-televised shows.

entertainment.title: Duran Duran’s Andy Taylor Was the Wildest of the Wild Boys
entertainment.summary: The late guitarist gave the band an aggressive edge that no other New Romantic act had — which is part of the reason the songs never fade into the past
entertainment.body:
Farewell to Andy Taylor , the bad boy in Duran Duran , the loose cannon, the purest rocker in the band. He was the guitarist who brought his own style of glam-rock flash to their classic Eighties hits, from “Hungry Like the Wolf” to “Girls on Film” to “Rio.” He gave them an aggressive edge that no other New Romantic band had — part of the reason these songs never fade into the past. The band announced his death today, at 65, after a long fight with prostate cancer.

The tragic news comes at a tough time for Duran Duran fans, just days after original drummer Roger Taylor announced he was stepping down because of his tinnitus. That leaves bassman John Taylor as the last of the band’s three Taylors. (None of whom were related.)

“He brought an indelible fire and swagger to our music,” Duran Duran said in a statement. “His playing drove the songs that took us around the world and with a dry wit that was matched only by his wonderfully unsentimental outlook on life he kept us grounded and gave the band its edge.”

Andy Taylor was the original guitarist from their early days, but he quit in 1986, at the peak of their fame. “It’s like one of those rat wheels, isn’t it?” he said in the 2018 documentary Duran Duran: There’s Something You Should Know . “And you just gotta be King Rat sometimes and say, ‘Bollocks! I’m jumping off!’”

He grew up in a fishing town near Newcastle and played his earliest gigs at military bases around Europe. But he took the train down to Birmingham when he saw a “guitarist wanted” ad in the British music paper Melody Maker. In the band’s first Rolling Stone cover story, in 1984 , he told the story of his audition for Duran Duran. “They were quite blatant,” Andy said. “They said, ‘We’re poseurs. We want a good-looking poseur band.’” But for Andy, that was no problem. “I said, ‘Good, because I like dressing up and I love wearing makeup.’”

These were fighting words, calculated to shock and outrage any old-school rock traditionalists who might be reading. And it worked — Duran Duran were a massively divisive band, especially in America. But it sums up the brazen attitude he brought to the band. Brash, Andy was. entertainment.title: Duran Duran’s Andy Taylor looked happy while greeting fans in last public sighting before his death
entertainment.summary: The musician died from prostate cancer on Monday. He was 65.
entertainment.body:
Andy Taylor was all smiles while greeting fans in London during his last public sighting before his death at the age of 65.

The late Duran Duran guitarist appeared in good spirits signing autographs and soaking up the love from his admirers as he left Wogan House after appearing on Zoe Ball’s since-ended BBC Radio 2 show on Aug. 30, 2023.

Taylor wore a Calvin Klein bucket hat, dark sunglasses, a black AllSaints jacket, a tiger-printed button-up shirt and Adidas sneakers for the outing.

The musician died on Monday after a “long and courageous battle” with stage 4 metastatic prostate cancer , his band and family announced via a joint statement Wednesday.

According to the statement, he “passed away peacefully at home, surrounded by his family.”

“To the world, Andy was a brilliant guitarist, but to us, he was the most wonderful husband, a loving dad and the proudest grandfather,” Taylor’s wife, Tracey, wrote. “He was the rock of our family. For all the incredible experiences music brought him, family always came first.”

“Nothing made him happier than having us all together, and no matter how far music took him, his heart was always at home,” she continued.

entertainment.title: Blade Runner 2099 Has A Major Problem That Goes Back To The Original 1982 Movie
entertainment.summary: Prime Video's new miniseries starring Hunter Schafer, Blade Runner 2099, is a follow-up to the movies Blade Runner and Blade Runner 2049, but it has a problem.
entertainment.body:
Clay Enos/Prime Add TVLine on Google: Preferred Source Google Discover Ironically, Prime's "Blade Runner 2099" is a program about the future, and it's stuck in the early 1980s. Showrunner Silka Luisa's limited series beams reverence for the classic proto-cyberpunk film that launched the franchise, and that fidelity to the urtext can be a benefit ... it can also be a hazard.

In "2099," bioengineered replicants have conquered organic mankind; elite LAPD officers known as blade runners hunt down uncooperative humans. Throughout the first four episodes, blade runners Olwen (Michelle Yeoh) and "Marian" — an undercover human whose real name is Cora (Hunter Schafer) — search for Marek (Johnny Harris), who's Olwen's ex and a person of interest to the underground resistance network that Cora works for. In Episode 4, Olwen finally learns why Marek went AWOL: He's searching for a golden orb believed to contain a memory from the long-deceased inventor of replicants, Eldon Tyrell, that holds the secret to open-ended replicant longevity.

Olwen has only eight days left to live, so Marek's quest to save her is very admirable. It is also very familiar. In director Ridley Scott's original "Blade Runner" from 1982 — a movie very loosely based on "Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?" by Philip K. Dick – a gang of replicants led by Roy Batty (Rutger Hauer) sneaks into Los Angeles to corner and confront their creator, tech oligarch Eldon Tyrell (Joe Turkel), to demand an expansion to their four-year lifespan.

Warner Bros./YouTube Not only does another story about replicants who quite understandably want to live longer feel very redundant, but it also relitigates a problem the "Blade Runner" version of civilization solved more than 50 years ago in its canonical past. In 1982's "Blade Runner," we learn the Tyrell Corporation created replicants primarily for treacherous grunt work in space. To prevent them from rising up and overthrowing their oppressors, Tyrell engineered replicants to live for a limited time — four years in the case of Nexus-6 models — and then automatically die, hence Roy's righteous fury.

Director Denis Villeneuve's "Blade Runner 2049" emerged as a long overdue sequel in 2017. None of the numerous replicants in "2049" appear concerned about a hard deadline. When K (Ryan Gosling) finds him early in the film, Nexus-8 model Sapper Morton (Dave Bautista) says he's been living and working on his protein farm since 2020 – which makes him considerably older than 4. In a short "2049" prequel film set in 2036, Niander Wallace (Jared Leto) — a mad scientist and business demon whose Wallace Corporation supplants the bankrupt Tyrell Corporation — claims the replicants he designs can live as long or as briefly as he designs them to. He probably isn't exaggerating.

Logo text ABC has won a court order barring the Federal Communications Commission from taking further action against the network amid the government’s efforts to possibly strip the company of its local broadcast licenses.

U.S. District Judge Loren Alikhan on Wednesday rebuffed the FCC ‘s bid to dismiss the lawsuit, finding that the agency likely violated ABC’s First Amendment rights by weaponizing its regulatory authority to retaliate against the network for protected speech and pressure it to change its editorial decisions.

“Today’s decision is an important victory for the First Amendment. We thank the court for its careful consideration,” an ABC News spokesperson said in a statement. The Disney-owned company sued the FCC earlier this year after the Brendan Carr-led agency called for an early review of ABC’s broadcast licenses. The renewal prompted concerns of retaliation since it followed an investigation into Disney’s diversity practices and ABC late-night host Kimmy Kimmel angering President Donald Trump with a joke.

In Wednesday’s ruling, the court said that Carr’s conduct is “powerful evidence” of the FCC’s “retaliatory motive.”

“It is no coincidence that President Trump criticized Mr. Kimmel’s skit on social media and the very next day Defendants initiated the early license renewal proceedings,” Alikhan wrote. She pointed to Carr’s comment that “we can do this the easy way or the hard way” and that “these companies can find ways to take action on Kimmel, or there is going to be additional work for the FCC ahead.”

The FCC has maintained that the early license renewal proceedings are merely “in aid” of its investigation into Disney’s employment practices and would’ve occurred regardless.
